verdictStatement: All five Codex v1 findings are genuinely repaired, and I measured each rather than reading the repair roster. The machine is now total and deterministic: I expanded the full 7x8 cross-product and found 36 declared pairs plus 20 falling to an explicit default-refuse, with exactly one pair carrying two transitions whose guards are mutually exclusive by construction. The continuation table resolves 342 of its 343 role-state triples explicitly, the 343rd falls fail-closed, and only three permissive outcomes exist — every one of them requiring CORE=ST-TRUSTED, so the 'permissive row while CORE is revoked' attack cannot be made to land. trustPolicyShape is referenced by all five transitions that enter or remain in TRUSTED. What withholds acceptance is one residual of the v1 nondeterminism blocker, narrowed but not eliminated: statePrecedence is written as an invariant over co-holding conditions, and the transition table enforces it only for EV-CLOCK out of ST-TRUSTED. A role that reaches ST-STALE-REVOCATION first and then expires stays in the less safety-dominant state, which is the surviving form of the exact harm Codex named — 'Event order therefore controls the visible state'. It escapes nothing and is audited, so it is not a blocker; it is a defect in the reviewed state machine that OBL-1 exists to deliver.

The refusal is an auditable attempted event.' v1's 32 undefined pairs with no default rule are gone.
repairVerification.determinism: MEASURED DETERMINISTIC. Exactly one pair — (ST-TRUSTED, EV-CLOCK) — carries two transitions, and their guards are mutually exclusive by construction: the ST-EXPIRED guard fires on 'Observed time >= metadataExpiry', and the ST-STALE-REVOCATION guard is explicitly conditioned 'AND EXPIRED guard does not hold'. No other pair is doubly covered. I also checked every from/on/to identifier against the declared state and event sets: zero dangling references.
repairVerification.codexSpecificsClosedOneByOne: Ordinary signed refresh now exists from EXPIRED/STALE-REVOCATION/QUORUM-LOST (transition 2), and ST-REVOKED is deliberately excluded with the guard saying so, so a revoked role can be healed only through the recovery path — correct, not an omission. EV-REVOKE now fires from TRUSTED/EXPIRED/STALE-REVOCATION/QUORUM-LOST/RECOVERY, closing Codex's 'a newer byte-valid EV-REVOKE has no transition to REVOKED'. EV-QUORUM-OBSERVE likewise. EV-RECOVER-COMMIT exists only from RECOVERY and refuses elsewhere by default. Recovery abort is explicit at transitions 3 and 8. The v1 wildcard EV-INSTALL target 'same or refuse' is replaced by two explicit rows, one of which says in terms 'Not a wildcard same or refuse'. FC-RECOVER's v1 'ST-*' is replaced by the five source states, and I confirmed that list is exactly transition 8's from-list.
repairVerification.residual: statePrecedence, the mechanism v2 introduced to answer Codex's precedence complaint, is not enforced by the table for two orderings. Recorded as S-1.

repairVerification.codexFinding: SITCV1-B2 — TRUSTED entry omits DR-112's half of the signature-validity split
repairVerification.howIMeasuredIt: I enumerated every transition whose target is ST-TRUSTED and checked each guard. All five invoke the new /trustPolicyShape: UNBOOTSTRAPPED+PAYLOAD, TRUSTED+PAYLOAD, [EXPIRED|STALE-REVOCATION|QUORUM-LOST]+PAYLOAD ('Same TRUSTED-entry predicate as first-bootstrap'), RECOVERY+RECOVER-COMMIT, and TRUSTED+INSTALL ('only while TRUSTED and trustPolicyShape still holds'). There is no path into or staying in TRUSTED that bypasses it.
repairVerification.theShapeAnswersEachNamedGap: Codex named six missing checks; trustPolicyShape supplies all six and one more. bootstrapAnchorCustody answers 'unauthorized/self-supplied root'; roleToKeyAndDelegatedNamespace answers 'wrong delegated namespace'; thresholdEvaluation answers signer threshold; revocationFreshness answers Codex's sharpest point, that a complete stale payload satisfied v1's guard while violating ST-TRUSTED's own definition; expiryAndFutureTime answers the future-issued-at bound; antiRollback is added on top.
repairVerification.boundaryRespected: envelopePreimageJoin is 'DECLARED and INACTIVE like RJ-4 ENVELOPE_MISMATCH'. I verified that against the accepted contract's own bytes: component-manifest-schemas.v2 RJ-4 lists UNSIGNED and DIGEST_MISMATCH as active subcodes and declares ENVELOPE_MISMATCH conditional and INACTIVE pending ID-DEP-1, and its ID-DEP-5 says 'trustMetadata stays reserved; TC-SIG's ceremony classes belong to DR-112's corpus'. So v2 takes the ceremony half that the accepted contract routes here and does not re-own the byte-level half. FC-TRUST-POLICY covers wrong-key, revoked-namespace, threshold-failure, stale-bootstrap and future-bootstrap. No number is minted; OD-112-1 and OD-112-2 stay RESERVED.

repairVerification.codexFinding: SITCV1-B3 — the offline-running policy is neither total nor conflict-resolved
repairVerification.howIMeasuredIt: I encoded the seven totalDecision rows and evaluated all 343 (CORE, INDEX, COMPONENT) triples under the declared CORE>INDEX>COMPONENT precedence. 342 match an explicit row; exactly one — CORE=TRUSTED, INDEX=UNBOOTSTRAPPED, COMPONENT=TRUSTED — falls to defaultRefuse and therefore refuses. Every gap Codex enumerated is now covered: the all-TRUSTED baseline is row 7, INDEX REVOKED/QUORUM-LOST is row 3, COMPONENT EXPIRED/STALE/QUORUM-LOST/RECOVERY is row 6, CORE EXPIRED/STALE/RECOVERY is rows 1-2.
repairVerification.theAttackThatCouldNotBeMadeToLand: Only three of the 343 triples yield a permissive outcome, and I checked each: all-TRUSTED (row 7), and INDEX EXPIRED or STALE-REVOCATION with CORE and COMPONENT both TRUSTED (row 4, already-running only). Every one requires CORE=ST-TRUSTED, and none involves any role in ST-REVOKED. So 'a continuation decision that prefers a permissive row while CORE is revoked' is impossible twice over — by the precedence rule and by row 4's own explicit CORE=TRUSTED conjunct. already-running is distinguished from new process throughout, and newly revoked replay is held at 'not designed' riding DR-113 rather than given a permissive answer.

repairVerification.codexFinding: SITCV1-S1 — refusals fall outside the transition-only audit contract
repairVerification.howIMeasuredIt: auditAndWaiver.audit now reads 'Every ATTEMPTED event — including guard failure and default refuse — appends { role, from, to, event, outcome: accepted|refused, refusalReason?, payloadDigests, clockObservation }. Stay-and-refuse records to == from.' That supplies the typed outcome, the refusal reason and the unchanged-state information Codex required, and it is cross-referenced from defaultTransition. FC-REFUSAL-AUDIT requires the negative fixtures to assert the record. Codex's caveat is honoured too: the record is kept as operational metadata and is explicitly 'not sealed evidence'.

shouldFix.title: statePrecedence is stated as an invariant but the transition table enforces it only for EV-CLOCK out of ST-TRUSTED
shouldFix.theInvariantAsWritten: 'When multiple refuse conditions hold, the visible state is the safety-dominant one: ST-REVOKED > ST-QUORUM-LOST > ST-EXPIRED > ST-STALE-REVOCATION > ST-RECOVERY > ST-TRUSTED > ST-UNBOOTSTRAPPED.'

instanceOne.measurement: (ST-STALE-REVOCATION, EV-CLOCK) is one of the 20 pairs with no declared transition, so it falls to defaultTransition: stay-in-state and refuse. The role therefore sits in ST-STALE-REVOCATION while the expiry condition also holds, and statePrecedence ranks ST-EXPIRED strictly above ST-STALE-REVOCATION. The invariant is violated.
instanceOne.whyItIsNotCaughtByTheArtifactsOwnFixture: FC-EVENT-ORDER tests only 'TRUSTED then CLOCK (expiry+stale both true) yields ST-EXPIRED'. That is the one ordering where the table happens to get it right, because transition 4's guard carries the tie-break. The ordering that breaks the invariant — stale first, expiry second — has no fixture.

instanceTwo.measurement: (ST-RECOVERY, EV-CLOCK) is likewise undeclared and defaults to stay. statePrecedence ranks ST-EXPIRED above ST-RECOVERY, so the invariant says the visible state should become ST-EXPIRED. Note that EV-REVOKE and EV-QUORUM-OBSERVE both DO list ST-RECOVERY in their from-sets, so REVOKED and QUORUM-LOST correctly preempt a ceremony in progress — expiry and staleness are the only two ranks that do not.
instanceTwo.whichHalfIsProbablyWrong: Here I think the table is right and the ordering is wrong: forcing a ceremony to ST-EXPIRED because the old metadata expired would abort recoveries that are underway precisely because metadata expired. That argues for demoting RECOVERY's rank or scoping the invariant, not for adding a transition.

shouldFix.whyThisIsTheRightSeverity: It is not a blocker. No permissive outcome is reachable through either gap: ST-EXPIRED and ST-STALE-REVOCATION are treated identically in every row of the continuation table, ST-RECOVERY refuses everywhere in that table, all three refuse EV-INSTALL, and the clock observation is itself audited under defaultTransition with outcome=refused and to==from, so the condition is recorded even though the label does not move. Nothing fails open. But it is more than advisory: the DR-112 acceptance cell's first fragment is 'Reviewed state machine', OBL-1 answers it at /machine, and this is the artifact stating a property of that machine which the machine does not have. It is also the narrowed survivor of the v1 blocker's stated harm — Codex wrote 'Event order therefore controls the visible state', and for these two orderings it still does. A conformance harness written from statePrecedence and one written from transitions[] would disagree.
shouldFix.minimumRepair: Either add the missing EV-CLOCK transitions so the table implements the ordering — (ST-STALE-REVOCATION, EV-CLOCK) -> ST-EXPIRED when the expiry guard holds is the one that clearly belongs — or scope the invariant to what the table actually enforces, e.g. 'statePrecedence governs guard selection where two declared transitions share a (state, event) pair, and the ranking of RECOVERY against EXPIRED/STALE-REVOCATION is deliberately not preemptive because a ceremony must survive expired predecessor metadata.' Either way, extend FC-EVENT-ORDER with the stale-then-expired ordering, since that is the vector that distinguishes the two readings.

advisories.title: The fixtureClasses roster entry says ADD, but an existing fixture was also edited
advisories.detail: The roster reads '/fixtureClasses (ADD FC-TRUST-POLICY, FC-CONTINUE-PRECEDENCE, FC-REFUSAL-AUDIT, FC-EVENT-ORDER)'. Those four are indeed added and no fixture was removed. But FC-RECOVER was also rewritten: v1's 'Install-scoped root recovery: ST-* -> ST-RECOVERY -> ST-TRUSTED; counters advance; executables do not move backward.' became v2's version naming the five source states and adding 'abort/refusal stays and is audited'. The parenthetical does not disclose it.
advisories.whyOnlyAdvisory: /fixtureClasses is on the closed roster, so the closing sentence is not falsified, and the edit itself is disclosed in substance by honestyRepairsFromV1[0], which names 'recovery abort' as part of the B1 repair. The edit also strengthens the fixture and directly answers Codex's complaint that 'FC-RECOVER says ST-* -> ST-RECOVERY although EV-RECOVER-BEGIN accepts only four of the seven states'. This is a single slip in a roster whose other four sub-path claims I verified as exactly correct.

advisories.title: The B1 repair summary overstates the from-sets of two events
advisories.detail: The summary says 'EV-REVOKE and EV-QUORUM-OBSERVE from every non-UNBOOTSTRAPPED state'. Measured: EV-REVOKE fires from five of the six non-UNBOOTSTRAPPED states, omitting ST-REVOKED; EV-QUORUM-OBSERVE fires from four, omitting ST-REVOKED and ST-QUORUM-LOST.
advisories.whyOnlyAdvisory: Both omissions are correct behaviour, not gaps. Re-revoking a revoked role and re-observing lost quorum from ST-QUORUM-LOST are no-ops that would either do nothing or violate statePrecedence, and defaultTransition covers them as audited stay-and-refuse. The machine is right; only the one-line summary of it is loose.
advisories.suggestedFix: '…from every non-UNBOOTSTRAPPED state except where the target is already at or above the resulting rank under statePrecedence.'

advisories.title: Two small irregularities in the continuation table
advisories.detail: First, the INDEX row enumerates ST-REVOKED, ST-QUORUM-LOST and ST-RECOVERY but omits ST-UNBOOTSTRAPPED, while the CORE row and the COMPONENT row both include UNBOOTSTRAPPED in their non-TRUSTED sets. That asymmetry is the sole reason any triple falls through: CORE=TRUSTED, INDEX=UNBOOTSTRAPPED, COMPONENT=TRUSTED is the one triple of 343 that reaches defaultRefuse. The outcome is correct and fail-closed, so nothing escapes; the enumeration is simply one member short of matching its siblings. Second, the CORE EXPIRED/STALE row says 'existing process may drain only if INDEX and COMPONENT still allow drain under later rows', which reads against the stated 'First fail-closed hit wins' precedence. The clause is defused by the same row's 'preview: refuse', so the preview decision stays total and deterministic.
advisories.whyOnlyAdvisory: Neither changes any outcome. Recorded because the deliverable is a decision table offered for review, and a reader reconstructing it will notice both.
advisories.suggestedFix: Add ST-UNBOOTSTRAPPED to the INDEX row so the table is explicit at 343 of 343, and move the drain clause into a forward-looking note so the precedence rule reads without exception.

attacksAttemptedAndFailed: That the machine is still partial. Full cross-product expansion refutes it: 56 of 56 pairs resolve, 20 of them through an explicit default-refuse rule that v1 lacked entirely.
That two transitions could fire for one (state, event) pair. Only one pair is doubly covered and its guards are complementary by construction.

That ordinary refresh still cannot heal expiry or staleness — Codex's v1 point. Transition 2 supplies exactly that path, and its deliberate exclusion of ST-REVOKED is stated in the guard rather than left as an omission.

That the exclusion of ST-REVOKED from EV-PRESENT-PAYLOAD strands a revoked role with no way out. It does not: EV-RECOVER-BEGIN lists ST-REVOKED among its five source states, so recovery is the only exit, which is the safe design.

That trustPolicyShape re-owns DR-103's byte-level verification. It does not — envelopePreimageJoin is held DECLARED and INACTIVE exactly as the accepted contract's RJ-4 holds ENVELOPE_MISMATCH, and I checked that against the accepted bytes.
That the monotonic-store citation is unresolvable. File 04 lines 78-79 are exactly the trust-roots/revocation/expiry/anti-rollback bullet claimed.
That a number was minted somewhere in the policy fields. Numeral extraction over seven policy objects returns only a gate id and a file number.
That a Codex v1 finding survives unrepaired. All five are closed; my S-1 is a narrowed residual of B1's precedence complaint, not an untouched finding.
coordinatorNote: This is a large and genuine repair — v1 had a machine that could not be reviewed and v2 has one that can, which is why my findings had to be produced by executing the machine rather than reading it. Three of the five Codex findings are closed completely and cleanly, and S2 was closed by both of the routes Codex offered rather than either. The single SHOULD-FIX is narrow and has no safety consequence: no permissive outcome is reachable, the affected states are treated identically downstream, and the event is audited. But it is a property the artifact asserts about its own central deliverable and does not hold, and it is the surviving trace of the v1 blocker's own words about event order controlling the visible state, so I do not think it should be carried past a successor. The three advisories are roster and enumeration hygiene. DR-112 remains OPEN, the subject remains CANDIDATE-NOT-APPLIED / DO-NOT-SEAL / binds NOTHING, and nothing in this verdict marks the row SATISFIED or authorizes docs/v2/implementation/.
